nodes.label: Median overlordship
nodes.full: After Urartu's fall the Armenian highlands came under the Median kings, whose power reached the Halys in 585 BC. Herodotus counts the Armenians among the peoples subject to the Medes, and Xenophon's Cyropaedia, a fiction, presents an Armenian king as a vassal of the Median Cyaxares. The Medes left no inscriptions or definite remains in the region.
nodes.src: Herodotus 1.72–73, 1.103; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 2.4; Zimansky, Ancient Ararat (1998).

nodes.label: Cyrus and the takeover
nodes.full: When Cyrus the Great overthrew Astyages in about 550 BC, the Median empire's peoples east and north, among them the Armenians, passed to Persian rule without a recorded conquest. The land appears as one of the Persian possessions thereafter, with a satrap and annual dues.
nodes.src: Herodotus 1.127–130; Nabonidus Chronicle; Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002).

nodes.label: Darius I and Armina
nodes.full: In the troubled accession of Darius I in 522–521 BC, Armenia, called Armina in Old Persian, Harminuya in Elamite and Urashtu in Akkadian, rose against him with the pretender-led revolts of the empire. The Behistun inscription records a series of battles fought for Darius by Dadarshish, an Armenian in his service, and by the Persian Vaumisa, ending in his victory in 521.
nodes.src: Behistun inscription (DB II 29–II 49, trilingual); Briant 2002; R. G. Kent, Old Persian (1953).

nodes.label: Armenian satrapy
nodes.full: Under Darius the empire was divided into satrapies; Herodotus's list puts the Armenians with the Pactyice and their neighbours as far as the Black Sea in the thirteenth, paying 400 silver talents, and the Matieni, Saspires and Alarodians (the Urartians) in the eighteenth, paying 200. The Persian satrap, often of the royal house, resided in the region with a garrison and a court.
nodes.src: Herodotus 3.93–94; Briant 2002; Amélie Kuhrt, The Persian Empire (2007).

nodes.label: Orontes and the Orontids
nodes.full: Xenophon names Orontes as the satrap of western Armenia in 401 BC, with Tiribazus in the east; Orontes, married to a daughter of Artaxerxes II, was long satrap of Armenia, and his descendants, the Orontids (Yervanduni in Armenian), are the first named dynasty of the land. An Orontes, perhaps the same man, appears later in Mysia and in the satraps' revolt of about 362 BC.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.5.17, 4.3.4, 4.4.4; Plutarch, Artaxerxes 27; Diodorus 15.91; Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Mithrenes
nodes.full: At Gaugamela the Armenians had been led by Orontes and Mithraustes; afterwards Alexander gave the satrapy to Mithrenes, the Persian noble who had surrendered Sardis to him. Alexander's armies did not themselves enter the highlands, and the Macedonian hold was thin.

nodes.label: Colchis and its gifts
nodes.full: The Colchians were not a regular satrapy; Herodotus says that they and the peoples as far as the Caucasus had been made to bring gifts every four years, a hundred boys and a hundred girls, and no tribute. Xenophon meets them as independent mountain warriors north of Trebizond. The Colchian kingdom of tradition was a loose chiefdom at the edge of the empire.
nodes.src: Herodotus 3.97; Xenophon, Anabasis 4.8; Lordkipanidze, Archäologie in Georgien (1991).

nodes.label: Moschi and Tibareni
nodes.full: Herodotus's nineteenth satrapy comprised the Moschi, Tibareni, Macrones, Mossynoeci and Mares, groups of the mountains south and east of the Black Sea; the Moschi are placed in the highlands of Meskheti, and many scholars take them to be among the ancestors of the Georgian tribes. Their tribute was 300 talents.

nodes.label: Taochoi
nodes.full: The Taochoi, whose land lay in the mountains of the upper Çoruh and Oltu rivers, appear in Xenophon as fortified farming communities under their own chiefs. They are the same people as the Diauehi or Tao of earlier and later sources, and the origin of the Georgian region of Tao.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.18, 4.7.1–19; Salvini, Geschichte und Kultur der Urartäer (1995).

nodes.label: Albanians and Caspians
nodes.full: The first named peoples in the east of the Caucasus are the Caspians (Herodotus, in the eleventh satrapy) and the Albanians, who fought at Gaugamela together with the Sacesinae under Persian command; Herodotus and Strabo place them between the Kura river and the sea and the mountains. Their land was apparently loosely tied to Persia.

nodes.label: Atropates
nodes.full: The Median commander Atropates fought at Gaugamela; Alexander made him satrap of Media in 328 BC, and the north-western part of Media, in what is today Iranian Azerbaijan and the lands towards the Araxes, was named Atropatene after him. The name became the Persian Adurbadagan and, much later, Azerbaijan, which was applied to the lands north of the Araxes only in the twentieth century.

nodes.label: Armenian rebellions
nodes.full: The Behistun inscription records that the Armenians rebelled against Darius, and that his general Dadarshish, 'an Armenian, my servant', fought them in a succession of battles, at Zuzza, Tigra and Uhyama, while Vaumisa fought in Assyria and later in Armenia. The rebel leader is not named.
nodes.src: Behistun inscription, DB II 29–49; Kent 1953; Briant 2002.

nodes.label: Xenophon crosses Armenia
nodes.full: After the defeat of Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa, some 10,000 Greek mercenaries led by Xenophon marched north from the Tigris through the Carduchian mountains and across the Armenian highlands in winter, with snow to the waist, losing men to frostbite and snow-blindness, and reached the Black Sea at Trebizond. Xenophon's account is the oldest eyewitness description of the region.

nodes.label: Fortress of the Taochoi
nodes.full: In the mountains of the Taochoi the Greeks found the people withdrawn into a hilltop stronghold with their goods, flocks and families, and took it in an assault in which, Xenophon says, the women threw their children over the cliffs and then leapt themselves, and many men did likewise. The Greeks gained food, the Taochians' stored supplies, and went on.

nodes.label: Xerxes’s army
nodes.full: Herodotus's catalogue of Xerxes's host in 480 BC lists the Armenians, armed like Phrygians and led by Artochmes, and the Colchians, Alarodians and Saspires, armed in the Colchian manner and commanded by Masistius. The names are a record of the contingents which the satrapies sent to the war.

nodes.label: Gaugamela
nodes.full: At Gaugamela Darius III's army included, on the left wing, the Medes under Atropates, the Albanians and Sacesinae, and the Armenians under Orontes and Mithraustes. Alexander broke the Persian line and Darius fled; the empire's remaining resistance collapsed in the following months.

nodes.label: Tribute list
nodes.full: Herodotus's list of Darius's twenty satrapies and what each paid, which has parallels in the monuments of Persepolis, gives for the Caucasian lands: the thirteenth, Armenians and neighbours, 400 talents; the eighteenth, Matieni, Saspires and Alarodians, 200; the nineteenth, Moschi, Tibareni and others, 300; and the eleventh, with the Caspians, 200 talents of silver. Silver was weighed in Babylonian talents.

nodes.label: Behistun inscription
nodes.full: The trilingual relief and text of Darius I on the cliff at Behistun in Iran, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, lists the provinces of the empire, among them Armina, and recounts the rebellions which he put down, including the Armenian. It is the first written source for the name of Armenia in its Persian form.

nodes.label: Iranian gods of Armenia
nodes.full: Under the long Persian rule Armenia took up the Iranian pantheon: Aramazd (Ahura Mazda), Mihr (Mithra), Anahit (Anahita), and Vahagn (Verethragna) are the chief gods of Armenian tradition, with temples and priestly families. Strabo, who describes the cult of Anaïtis at Acilisene, says that the Armenians worship the Persian gods.
nodes.src: Strabo 11.14.16; Movses Khorenatsi, History 2.12–14 (later); James Russell, Zoroastrianism in Armenia (1987).

nodes.label: Sanctuary of Vani
nodes.full: On the hill of Vani in the Rioni valley an urban sanctuary of terraces, altars and a temple was built in the sixth century BC and flourished in the fifth and fourth; the offerings of gold, bronze, clay figurines and Greek pottery found there are the finest evidence of religion in Colchis. The site was explored by Otar Lordkipanidze from 1947.
nodes.src: O. Lordkipanidze, Vani excavation reports (1947–); Lordkipanidze 1991.

nodes.label: Armenians at the Apadana
nodes.full: On the stairs of the Apadana at Persepolis, delegations of twenty-three peoples bring gifts to the king; in one the Armenians, in tall caps and Persian dress, lead a horse and carry a large vessel, a theme in keeping with the satrapy's tribute in horses. The identification of some delegations is debated.
nodes.src: Apadana reliefs, Persepolis (eastern stairway); Briant 2002; Margaret Root, The King and Kingship in Achaemenid Art (1979).

nodes.label: Xerxes’s inscription at Van
nodes.full: Xerxes had an inscription in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, cut into a smoothed panel on the cliff of Van Fortress, beside the niche of Argishti I of Urartu, in which he proclaims his father Darius and his dominion by Ahuramazda's grace. It is the only Achaemenid royal inscription in the highlands.

nodes.label: Colchian gold
nodes.full: Rich burials at Vani and the Greek–Colchian cemetery at Pichvnari on the coast contain gold earrings and diadems of filigree, silver vessels, bronze figures and Attic and East Greek pottery, mixing local and Greek taste. Many are among the most remarkable objects of Georgian archaeology and are in the national museum.
nodes.src: Lordkipanidze 1991; Pichvnari excavation reports (Kacharava and Kvirkvelia); Georgian National Museum.

nodes.label: Xenophon’s Armenia
nodes.full: Xenophon describes the Armenians he met in winter: villages of underground houses entered by ladders, with a passage for the livestock; stores of wheat, barley, vegetables and pulses; wine in mixing bowls and barley beer drunk through reeds; the chiefs who give hospitality; and sacred horses dedicated to the Sun. It is the earliest ethnography of the Armenian villagers.

nodes.label: Herodotus and Hecataeus
nodes.full: Greek geographers placed the Phasis and the Caucasus at the limit of the known world: Hecataeus of Miletus drew the Black Sea and its eastern coast, and Herodotus describes the Caucasus as a great range with a mixed population and the Caspian as a closed sea, with the Araxes flowing to it. They knew the peoples only by their names.

nodes.label: Iranian words in Armenian
nodes.full: Armenian has an unusually large Iranian vocabulary, which for long led to its being classed as an Iranian language; in 1875 the German linguist Heinrich Hübschmann showed that its core is a separate branch of Indo-European, with Iranian words borrowed. The loans include terms of court, religion, law and the army, and reflect centuries of Persian and Parthian dominance, beginning in this period.
nodes.src: Heinrich Hübschmann, 'Ueber die Stellung des Armenischen im Kreise der indogermanischen Sprachen', Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung 23 (1875); Robert Hewsen.

nodes.label: Armenos of Thessaly
nodes.full: Greek writers of the Alexander period explained the name Armenia as that of a Thessalian, Armenos of Armenion, who was said to have followed Jason or to have been one of Alexander's companions and to have settled the land. The story, preserved by Strabo from Alexander's historians, is a Greek invention; the name derives from the Old Persian Armina.
nodes.src: Strabo 11.14.12 (citing Medius of Larissa and Cyrsilus of Pharsalus).

nodes.label: Twenty thousand foals
nodes.full: Armenia, with the neighbouring Media, was the great horse-breeding land of the empire, and Strabo says its satrap sent the king 20,000 foals each year at the feast of Mithra, the Mithrakana. The silver tribute and the horses made the highlands one of the empire's richest northern provinces.

nodes.label: Wine, barley, highland farm
nodes.full: The Armenian villages Xenophon passed grew wheat, barley and legumes, kept sheep, goats, cattle and fowl and made wine and barley beer, in a farming system whose crop mix had come down from the Urartian period. The harsh winters and short seasons made storage essential.

nodes.label: Trade of the Phasis
nodes.full: Greek traders from Miletus, Sinope and later Athens sailed to the Colchian coast for timber, flax, pitch, wax, honey and metal and brought wine, olive oil and fine pottery. Attic pottery of the fifth and fourth centuries fills the graves at Pichvnari and the Greek trading town grew into an entrepôt.

nodes.label: Colchian coins
nodes.full: In the sixth or fifth century BC the Colchian chiefs began to mint silver coins of a distinctive type, known to Georgians as 'kolkhidki', with a bull's head and a stamped reverse, among the earliest coins of the Caucasus. Persian darics and sigloi also reached the highlands, and are found in hoards in Armenia and Georgia.
nodes.src: David Lang and G. Dundua on Georgian numismatics; Lordkipanidze 1991.

nodes.label: Colchian iron
nodes.full: The Colchian smiths continued to make axes, sickles, knives and weapons in iron, together with bronze ornaments and gold work, in the workshops of the Rioni valley and the coastal towns, and their products reached the Greek market. The metalworking tradition continued from the earlier Iron Age.
nodes.src: Lordkipanidze 1991; Sagona, The Archaeology of the Caucasus (2018).

nodes.label: Royal Road through Armenia
nodes.full: Herodotus describes the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, which passed across Cilicia, then into Armenia where it ran 56½ parasangs with fifteen stations and military guards, and through the crossing of four navigable rivers, before entering Matiene and Cissia. Persian garrisons and post stations tied the highlands to the empire.

nodes.label: Pichvnari
nodes.full: The cemetery of Pichvnari near Kobuleti on the Black Sea contains several hundred graves, Colchian and Greek side by side, for a mixed community of local people and Greek settlers from the sixth to the fourth century, with Attic black-figure and red-figure vases, amphorae and jewellery of both traditions.
nodes.src: Pichvnari excavations (Kacharava and Kvirkvelia, 1967–); Pichvnari exhibition catalogue.

nodes.label: Persian frontier and Alexander
nodes.full: For two centuries the Caucasus formed the northern frontier of the Achaemenid empire, a zone of satrapies in the south and of loosely tied hill peoples in the north and west. After Gaugamela Alexander took the Persian capitals in 330 BC; his generals did not subdue the Caucasus and the highlands passed to successor rulers who had a free hand.

nodes.label: Villagers in underground houses
nodes.full: Xenophon's account of the village headman, who entertained the Greek officers and fed their men, of houses dug into the earth with a ladder for the family and a ramp for the animals, and of the long winter shut-in, is the closest view of ordinary highland life from this period.

nodes.label: Children as gifts
nodes.full: The gift of 100 boys and 100 girls every four years from the Colchians and their neighbours, as Herodotus reports, would have meant the taking of several thousand children over the empire's rule, to serve at court or as eunuchs and slaves. Nothing is known about the children's lives.

nodes.label: Rhodogune
nodes.full: Orontes the satrap of Armenia was married to Rhodogune, a daughter of Artaxerxes II, a marriage which tied the satrap closely to the royal house and underpinned the Orontid claim to later royal status. Plutarch records the marriage but little else of Rhodogune.

nodes.label: Urartu’s fall and the Median state
nodes.full: The Urartian kingdom ended in the early sixth century BC and the highland lands fell to the Median state, which by 585 BC had reached the Halys river.
nodes.src: background — see the Urartu and Colchis folio (urartu-colchis-1200bc-585bc)
